Topic: Dandelin Spheres: The 3D Secret Behind Conic Sections

Target audience: High school students (Advanced Geometry) and early undergraduate students

Section: section_1 — The Mystery of the Slice

Lecture lines:
Imagine slicing a cone with a flat plane.
This intersection creates a perfect elliptical curve.
Why does this slice follow the ellipse formula?

Planned animations:
Fade in a 3D cone (#888888) and a slicing plane (#FFFFFF) at an angle.
Draw the intersection curve (the slice) in bright cyan (#00FFFF).
Rotate the camera to show the slice is an oval shape on the plane.
Fade out the cone and plane, leaving only the cyan oval.
Center the cyan oval and add text 'Why is this an Ellipse?' (#FFFFFF).

Section: section_2 — Prerequisite: The String & The Sphere

Lecture lines:
Ellipses have two foci with constant distance sum.
Tangents from one point to a sphere are equal.
These rules help unlock the cone's secret.

Planned animations:
Draw a cyan ellipse (#00FFFF) with two red dots (#FF0000) labeled 'Foci'.
Draw two yellow lines (#FFFF00) from a point on the curve to the foci; show their sum is constant.
Show a blue sphere (#0000FF) and demonstrate that all tangent segments from an external point to it are equal length (#00FF00).

Section: section_3 — The Magic Trick: Inserting the Spheres

Lecture lines:
Nest two spheres between the cone and plane.
Plane contact points will become our two foci.
We call these the Dandelin Spheres.

Planned animations:
Re-display the 3D cone (#888888) and slicing plane (#FFFFFF).
Insert a small sphere (#FFD700) above the plane, tangent to both the cone and the plane.
Mark its contact point on the plane as 'F1' (#FF0000).
Insert a larger sphere (#FFD700) below the plane, tangent to both.
Mark its contact point on the plane as 'F2' (#FF0000).

Section: section_4 — The Geometric Bridge

Lecture lines:
Pick any point P on the ellipse's edge.
Link P to the sphere's contact point.
Trace from P along the cone's surface.
These two segments are equal tangent lengths.
This bridge connects the plane and cone.

Planned animations:
Pick a point 'P' (#FFFFFF) on the intersection curve.
Draw a line from 'P' to 'F1' and a line along the cone to where the top sphere touches it.
Highlight these two segments in orange (#FFA500) to show they are equal tangent lengths.

Section: section_5 — The Grand Proof

Lecture lines:
Sum the distances from P to both foci.
This sum equals a fixed cone slant distance.
Slant distance between spheres never changes.
Thus, the total distance from P is constant.
This proves the curve is a perfect ellipse.

Planned animations:
Show that PF1 equals the segment from P to the top circle (Q1).
Show that PF2 equals the segment from P to the bottom circle (Q2).
Combine these to show PF1 + PF2 = Q1Q2, which is the slant distance between the two circles.
Slide point P around the ellipse; show the distance Q1Q2 between circles stays constant.
Display 'Constant Sum = Ellipse' (#FFFFFF) with a celebratory glow on the curve.

Section: section_6 — Application: From Ice Cones to Orbits

Lecture lines:
Tilting the plane creates other conic sections.
This geometry governs how planets orbit stars.
3D shapes explain our 2D mathematical world.

Planned animations:
Tilt the slicing plane to show a Parabola (#FF00FF) and a Hyperbola (#00FF00).
Transform the scene into a planet (#ADD8E6) orbiting a sun (#FFFF00) in an elliptical path.
Final text: 'The Geometry of the Universe' (#FFFFFF).
